seo.description: Voiceover production support for LSPs, eLearning teams and publishers. Discuss narration scripts, target languages, audio specifications and delivery requirements.

hero.title: Voiceover Services for eLearning & Multimedia Localization
hero.lead: Voiceover production and multilingual narration support for localization service providers, eLearning teams, publishers and digital-content businesses.
paragraphs: Voiceover-related production for supported eLearning and multimedia projects, with scripts, voices, recording arrangements and audio outputs defined by the brief.

lead.text: A voiceover project may begin with an approved script in the source language or translated scripts prepared for particular audiences.
The audio may need to follow an established tone, use approved terminology and fit within the timing of a course, animation or video.

For international localization projects, voiceover production can be one stage in a wider process involving script preparation, translation, linguistic approval, recording, editing, media synchronization and final delivery.
These activities do not always belong to the same supplier.
EPUBTRANS supports voiceover-related production as an individual assignment or as a separately scoped component of multimedia or eLearning localization.

blocks.text: Learning content may require spoken explanations that support learners as they follow demonstrations, activities, presentations or other instructional material.
Voiceover production for this content can be assessed against the supplied scripts, learning objectives and media requirements.
Relevant applications include:
A course may require one continuous narration or multiple recordings associated with individual screens, scenes or modules.
The number of audio assets, naming rules and playback requirements should be established before production.
Some projects require equivalent narration in several target languages.
Depending on the source materials and agreed scope, production may involve coordinating language-specific scripts, voice requirements, recording arrangements and final audio assets.
The project should identify:

items: Gender or voice characteristics where relevant to the brief

blocks.text: Current language coverage, dialect support and voice-talent availability must be confirmed for each assignment.
EPUBTRANS does not assume that every requested voice or language combination is available within every production schedule.
A script that works well as written text may require review before being recorded.
Spoken narration can raise questions about pronunciation, abbreviations, symbols, technical terminology and the length of translated phrases.
Depending on the agreed scope, relevant preparation may involve:

items: Reviewing supplied scripts for recording readiness
Recording pronunciation instructions supplied by the client
Confirming the treatment of acronyms and numbers
Identifying content associated with individual screens or scenes
Flagging text that may not fit within the available audio duration
Organizing approved scripts for the specified recording workflow

blocks.text: Language adaptation and changes to meaning require appropriate linguistic or client approval.
Translation, transcreation, script rewriting and subject-matter verification are separate activities unless expressly included.
A project may require a particular narration style, language variant or voice profile.
The recording approach can depend on talent availability, the desired delivery style, production budget and technical requirements.
Where voice talent or recording services are part of the assignment, the available options, responsibilities and arrangements must be confirmed before production.
This may involve obtaining approved voice samples, defining recording instructions and agreeing how the selected voice will be used.
EPUBTRANS's documented service scope does not establish that all voices are permanently available in-house or that every project uses an EPUBTRANS-owned studio.
The agreement should identify any third-party talent, recording arrangements, usage rights and required approvals.
Recorded narration may need preparation before delivery to a client or integration into another multimedia asset.
Depending on the agreed production capabilities and technical brief, possible tasks include:

items: Reviewing recorded speech against the approved script
Identifying unwanted pauses or recording issues
Organizing audio by scene, lesson or module
Preparing files for the required destination workflow
Managing approved re-recording or correction requests

blocks.text: Audio cleanup, mixing, mastering, noise reduction and other post-production tasks require separate scope confirmation.
The appropriate processing method should reflect the original recording quality and the receiving platform's requirements.
A narrated course or video may have a defined duration for each section.
Different target languages can require more or less time to communicate the same meaning.
Where timing requirements apply, voiceover production may involve reviewing the expected duration, preparing suitable recording segments and flagging passages that exceed the available time.
The required synchronization approach should be specified before production.
Precise lip synchronization, replacement dialogue, video editing and changes to animations are not automatically included in a standard narration assignment.
Clients may already have voiceover recordings that need updating.
Examples include changes to a product name, revised training instructions, a corrected phrase or an updated course module.
EPUBTRANS can assess applicable audio correction requirements based on the available recordings, source scripts and recording arrangements.
Replacing a small portion of an existing recording may require access to the original performer and compatible recording conditions.
Continuity of voice, tone or technical characteristics cannot be assumed when the original production assets or talent are unavailable.

lead.text: Localization service providers and translation agencies often manage multilingual projects involving several specialized production stages.
A client may supply approved translations and require a separate partner to help prepare the corresponding spoken audio.
EPUBTRANS can assess voiceover production needs within these workflows while respecting the responsibilities of the commissioning LSP.

blocks.text: Where the client provides final translated scripts, the voiceover assignment can focus on the agreed recording and audio-delivery requirements.
Questions about terminology, pronunciation or meaning should be referred to the designated linguistic reviewer or client.
Language variants, accents and culturally appropriate spoken conventions can affect the intended narration.
The project brief should identify the target locale and any specific voice requirements rather than relying only on a broad language name.
A multilingual project may involve files moving between translators, linguistic reviewers, recording providers, audio editors and eLearning production teams.
The handoff should establish which party owns the approved script, selects or approves the voice, handles corrections and integrates the final files.
EPUBTRANS's role is determined by the commissioned production scope; the LSP can retain the wider client relationship and language-management responsibilities.

lead.text: These terms are related but should not be treated as interchangeable.

blocks.text: Voiceover commonly provides commentary, instructions or translated narration over a video or other visual content.
It may need to follow the pacing of the media without matching the visible lip movements of an on-screen speaker.
Dubbing may involve replacing existing dialogue with a performance in another language.
Some dubbing projects require matching dialogue timing, character performance and visible mouth movements.
These tasks can involve different recording and video-production requirements from ordinary narration.
Lip-sync dubbing, character casting and dialogue replacement require separate capability and scope confirmation.
Audio description communicates important visual information to people who cannot see the video adequately.
Its content is written for a different purpose from conventional narration or translated voiceover.
A project requiring audio description may need specialist scripting, recording and integration, along with review against applicable accessibility requirements.
Standard voiceover production should not be described as automatically providing audio description or compliance with accessibility standards.
For broader accessibility-related publishing requirements, refer to our Accessibility Services.
Courses may contain narration synchronized with slides, animations, demonstrations or interactive content.
Project requirements can include audio files for individual screens, language-specific versions, pronunciation guidance and synchronization with existing course timing.
Importing recordings into Storyline, Rise, Lectora or another authoring environment must be defined separately from the audio-production assignment.
Educational publishers may use voiceover in teaching videos, digital textbooks, recorded explanations, learning resources or other multimedia content.
Specialist terminology and subject-specific pronunciation may require approved guidance from an editor or subject-matter reviewer.
Full-length audiobook narration and production, where requested, should be separately assessed because of differences in duration, talent rights, recording requirements and editorial review.
Organizations may require narration for employee onboarding, compliance training, technical demonstrations, product education or internal presentations.
The appropriate voice, delivery style and audio structure depend on the material and its intended audience.
Video-localization assignments may involve approved translated narration alongside source video, visual assets and supporting language files.
The scope must specify whether EPUBTRANS is expected to deliver audio only or undertake any separately commissioned synchronization or media integration.

lead.text: Voiceover recordings need to be prepared for the intended downstream system.
Audio-production specifications may include:

items: Separate files for scenes, slides or modules
Agreed audio level or processing requirements

lead.text: WAV and MP3 are examples of common audio formats used in multimedia workflows.
These examples do not establish that every specification or encoding configuration is currently supported by EPUBTRANS.

blocks.text: An eLearning project may require separate files for each module, slide or interaction.
The file list and naming convention should be supplied or approved in advance.
Other projects may need a single narration file or a defined set of longer recordings.
The expected duration, speaker arrangement and edit requirements should be identified before production.
A valid audio file does not automatically guarantee correct playback or synchronization in every video platform or eLearning application.
Importing the audio, changing animations, producing final video files and testing the complete learning package are separate tasks unless expressly commissioned.

lead.text: A clear project brief helps define the recording and production requirements.

blocks.text: Depending on the assignment, useful information may include:

items: Number and preferred characteristics of voices
Target audience and preferred speaking style
Number of lessons, videos or modules
Voice samples or reference styles, if available
Required audio formats and technical specifications

blocks.text: Not every item applies to every project.
A draft translation, an approved recording script and a final timed script are not necessarily the same deliverable.
Unresolved terminology, missing source context or significant changes after approval can affect recording and correction work.
Before voiceover production begins, the commissioning client should identify who can authorize script changes and approve the final spoken text.
The client should have appropriate rights to use the supplied materials.
Where voice talent, music, recordings or licensed audio assets are involved, permitted uses, distribution territories, duration and other relevant licence terms may require agreement.
These matters should be clarified before production rather than assumed to be included in a standard voiceover quotation.

lead.text: The agreed outputs depend on the project.
Possible deliverables include:

items: Audio divided into agreed scenes, screens or modules
Audio files in the approved technical format
Associated scripts or recording notes, where contracted
Agreed file lists and version information
Issue or pronunciation query lists, where commissioned

lead.text: The delivery specification should identify the number of voices, languages, files, formats and review stages.
Translated scripts, full audio mastering, video editing, precise dubbing, LMS integration and accessibility testing are not automatically part of every voiceover assignment.
Editable audio-production project files or original recording sessions should be included only where supported and expressly agreed.

groups.title: 1. Review the Scripts and Media Requirements

blocks.text: We review representative scripts, target languages, source media, intended audience and technical requirements.
Any timing constraints, missing translations, terminology questions or voice-selection dependencies are identified.
The project requirements define voice characteristics, supported languages, recording arrangements, audio specifications and expected deliverables.
Responsibilities for voice approval, linguistic review, audio processing, synchronization and final client acceptance are agreed.
Scripts and pronunciation guidance are organized for the agreed workflow.
Questions about wording or specialist terminology are referred to the designated reviewers before recording where possible.

groups.title: 4. Coordinate the Agreed Recording and Audio Work

blocks.text: Voice talent, recording and editing activities are arranged only within the capabilities and services confirmed for the assignment.
The commissioned narration is prepared according to the approved script and production brief.
Review may cover completeness, pronunciation against approved guidance, audio issues, file structure and other requirements included in the project scope.
Where linguistic or technical concerns require client decisions, queries are recorded for review.
Completed recordings and agreed supporting files are organized for the specified handoff.
Corrections, re-recording, video integration and additional review stages are managed according to the agreed arrangement.

lead.text: Voiceover quality should be assessed against the actual project brief, not an unsupported promise of perfect performance.
Depending on the scope, relevant checks may include:

items: Consistency with the approved delivery instructions

blocks.text: The commissioning client or its designated linguistic reviewer should confirm the accuracy of translated scripts and terminology.
Recording-production QA does not automatically include independent translation review or subject-matter verification.
The client should identify who will approve the proposed voice style or voice sample when voice selection is part of the work.
Changes to an already approved voice direction may have implications for recording and revision scope.
Where commissioned and supported, technical checks may address the specified audio properties and delivery structure.
The exact recording, processing and validation methods should be identified.
A technically suitable audio file may still require additional work to fit the final video or learning experience.
Ordinary narration alone does not establish that the complete media is accessible or compatible with every receiving platform.
Final integration, end-to-end testing and publication acceptance remain separate responsibilities unless agreed.

sections.title: What Affects Voiceover Project Scope and Scheduling?

blocks.text: Longer scripts, specialist terminology, complex pronunciation or incomplete source materials can increase production effort.
The number of languages and requested accents affects the available production options and review requirements.
A single narrator differs from a multi-speaker or character-based recording assignment.
Talent availability, selection and licensing arrangements should be confirmed before scheduling.
Simple narration delivery can differ significantly from projects requiring substantial editing, mixing, mastering or other audio preparation.
Narration that must fit fixed slide or video durations may require additional planning and client-approved script adjustments.
Changes to scripts after recording, additional voice auditions or repeated revisions can affect the agreed scope.
The intended channels, territories, usage duration and licensing requirements may influence talent and recording arrangements.
These factors are reviewed before discussing project estimates and delivery schedules.

lead.text: Each service is separately scoped. The inclusion of voiceover work does not automatically include transcription, translation, subtitles or full multimedia integration.

blocks.text: Subtitle timing, segmentation and timed-text production for approved video and multilingual content.
Converting recorded speech into readable text and other agreed transcript outputs.
Localization production for digital courses, course assets and supported eLearning authoring workflows.
Document layout and formatting for multilingual publication and localization workflows.
Accessibility-related production and remediation for supported documents, eBooks and digital publishing content.

groups.title: What does EPUBTRANS's Voiceover Services offering include?

blocks.text: EPUBTRANS's documented localization production portfolio includes voiceover-related workflows and contracted narration assets. Specific recording, talent, editing and delivery activities are defined for each project.

Multilingual voiceover requirements can be assessed using the target languages, approved scripts and specified voice profiles. Current talent availability and language coverage must be confirmed before accepting a project.

groups.title: Do you have your own recording studio and voice artists?

blocks.text: The current website describes studio recording and voice artists, but the available internal documentation does not confirm the present in-house or partner delivery model. Recording arrangements and talent options should be verified for each assignment.

groups.title: Can you work with translated scripts supplied by our LSP?

blocks.text: Yes, client-supplied, approved translated scripts can form the basis of a scoped voiceover workflow. Linguistic review and script changes remain subject to the agreed responsibilities.

groups.title: Is translation included in voiceover production?

blocks.text: Not automatically. Script translation, transcreation and linguistic approval should be commissioned or supplied separately as needed.

groups.title: Can you prepare narration for eLearning modules?

blocks.text: Narration for eLearning content can be assessed using the approved scripts, module structure, audio requirements and target languages. Integration into course-authoring files is a separate requirement unless commissioned.

groups.title: What is the difference between voiceover and dubbing?

blocks.text: Voiceover typically provides narration or commentary without requiring a precise match to visible mouth movements. Dubbing may involve replacing dialogue and more demanding performance or synchronization requirements.
Lip-sync dubbing requires additional voice, recording and video synchronization capabilities. EPUBTRANS must confirm current support and the full production scope before agreeing to such work.

groups.title: Which audio file formats do you deliver?

blocks.text: WAV and MP3 are common audio-delivery formats. The currently supported encoding settings and output formats must be confirmed against the project specification.

groups.title: Can you synchronize narration with our video or eLearning course?

blocks.text: Timing and synchronization requirements can be reviewed, but the agreement should distinguish preparing suitably timed audio from editing video, modifying animations or integrating files into a course package.

groups.title: Do you offer AI-generated voices or voice cloning?

blocks.text: No AI voice-generation or cloning capability is assumed. Any such request would require separate technical feasibility, explicit voice rights and consent, and approval of the intended use.

groups.title: Is ordinary voiceover the same as audio description for accessibility?

blocks.text: No. Audio description communicates important visual information to people who cannot see it adequately. Its scripting, recording and accessibility requirements differ from ordinary narration.

groups.title: Can you provide a voice sample and guarantee the same voice for future updates?

blocks.text: Voice sample availability, licensing and future talent continuity depend on the recording arrangement. The same performer or recording conditions cannot be guaranteed without a separate agreement.

groups.title: What information is required for a voiceover quotation?

blocks.text: Please provide the approved scripts, language and locale requirements, approximate duration, voice preferences, source media, pronunciation guidance, audio specifications, usage requirements and preferred schedule.
